body.p: This summer, Hollins Park Wildlife Centre is holding its first ever Panda Week. For nine days, our two red pandas, Juniper and Tao, will be the stars of the park. We think they are the most charming animals you will ever meet.

Red pandas live in mountain forests in the Himalayas and south-west China. They are about the size of a large house cat and have a long, ringed tail, which helps them balance in the trees. Like giant pandas, they eat mostly bamboo. Despite the shared name, the two animals are not closely related.
All Panda Week activities are included in the normal entry price.

ul: Adult: £14.50
Under 3: free
Family (2 adults and 2 children): £42.00

body.p: Save 10% when you book online at least one day before your visit.

ul: Red pandas are shy. Please keep your voice low on the Bamboo Walk.
Flash photography is not allowed near the panda enclosure.
The Bamboo Walk has steps. A step-free route is signposted from the Visitor Hub.

texts.title: We went to Panda Week. Was it worth it?

body.p: Last Saturday, my partner, our two children and I spent the day at Hollins Park for Panda Week. I'll be honest: I wasn't sure a whole week about two small animals would be worth the drive. I was wrong.

We arrived just before the 10:30 feeding talk, and it was the best part of the day. The keeper explained that bamboo gives red pandas very little energy, so they have to eat a lot of it. My eight-year-old hasn't stopped talking about it since.

By the afternoon, things were less exciting. Tao was nowhere to be seen, and Juniper slept on a high branch for the whole of the 14:00 question time. The Bamboo Walk was also very crowded, and we struggled to hear the keeper over the noise.
Booking online the day before saved us a few pounds on our family ticket, which helped, because the café prices were shocking: nearly £4 for a small juice.
My advice? Go early and take a packed lunch. The morning was magical. The afternoon was mostly a sleeping ball of fur.

texts.title: Five days in Israel: desert and coast

body.p: Join a small group of no more than 12 travellers for five relaxed days exploring the coast and the desert of Israel. You'll stay in friendly guesthouses, eat fresh local food and travel in a comfortable air-conditioned minibus.

Where
Highlights

Morning float in the Dead Sea. Transfer to the airport.

ul: Every guide has lived in Israel for at least ten years.

texts.title: A month of eating (and waiting for buses) in Israel

body.p: Everyone told me the food would be good. Nobody told me it would ruin every other breakfast for me. Shakshuka, eggs cooked in a rich tomato and pepper sauce, is now my idea of the perfect start to the day.

Lunch was usually falafel stuffed into a warm pitta with salad and tahini, bought from a small stall. The best one I had was in a side street near the market in Tel Aviv, where the owner refused to let me leave without trying his hummus too.

Getting around was easier than I expected. The train along the coast is quick and clean, and buses reach most towns. One warning, though: from Friday afternoon until Saturday evening, many buses and trains stop running for Shabbat, the weekly day of rest. I learned this the hard way, and spent a very long Friday evening at a bus stop that no bus was ever going to visit.
If I went back, I'd skip the organised tours and travel on my own. You see more, you spend less, and you eat better.

body.p: From 6 April, the number 14 bus between Kettlewick and Fennbridge will follow a new route. We have made these changes after a public consultation last autumn, when more than 600 people told us what they need from their local buses.

ul: The 14 will no longer go along Mill Lane. Instead, it will stop at the new Kettlewick Health Centre.
A new 14A service will run on Sundays only, every two hours.
The first bus on weekdays will leave Kettlewick 20 minutes earlier, at 06:10.
The bus stops on Mill Lane will be removed. The nearest stop will be on Station Road, about 300 metres away.

body.h: New weekday timetable: Kettlewick to Fennbridge

body.p: Buses then run every hour, at 10 minutes past the hour, until 18:10. Journeys between 08:00 and 09:00 take longer because of school traffic.
Single and return prices are not changing. The Vale Day Ticket (£5.20) can be used on all our routes, including the new 14A.
We will review the new route after six months. Tell us what you think by emailing buses@valeoffenn.example or by picking up a feedback card on any bus.
Dear Editor,

I am writing about the council's decision to take the 14 bus away from Mill Lane. The council says the nearest stop will be "about 300 metres away". That may sound like nothing, but Station Road is at the top of a steep hill, and many people on Mill Lane are in their eighties.

The council also says that more than 600 people took part in its consultation. I have spoken to my neighbours, and not one of them knew it was happening. It was only advertised online, which is no use to people who do not use the internet.
I will admit that a stop at the new health centre is a good idea. My own doctor has moved there, and at the moment I need two buses to reach it. But surely the bus could do both?
I would ask the council to keep at least one stop on Mill Lane, even if the bus only goes that way a few times a day.
Yours faithfully,
A Mill Lane resident

texts.title: Hawsden or Brayminster? A guide for people moving to the area

body.p: Every year, hundreds of families move into Brayminster District. Many of them face the same question: should we live in the market town of Brayminster, or in one of the villages around it, such as Hawsden? This guide sets out the facts to help you decide.

head: Hawsden (village)
Brayminster (town)
rows: One village shop and post office
Two supermarkets and a high street
Three primary schools and one secondary school
A surgery open two mornings a week
A health centre open six days a week
Every two hours, Monday to Saturday
None. The nearest is in Brayminster, 6 miles away.
Yes, with trains to the city

body.p: Hawsden has mostly older detached and semi-detached houses, many with large gardens. Very few homes come up for sale or rent, so you may have to wait. Brayminster has a wider mix, including flats, terraced houses and a new estate of 300 homes on the edge of town.

ul: If you do not drive, village life can be harder, because buses are less frequent.
Village life can be quieter, and many people say they feel part of a close community.
In our view, Brayminster offers the best of both worlds: town services, with the countryside on your doorstep.

texts.title: Six months in a village: what nobody tells you

body.p: When we moved from a flat in the city to a cottage in Hawsden, I pictured long walks, fresh air and friendly neighbours. I got all three. I also got a two-hour wait for the bus, a phone signal that disappears if you stand in the wrong room, and a village shop that closes at five.

Don't get me wrong. I love it here. In our first week, three neighbours knocked on the door with cake, and the woman next door now feeds our cat when we're away. In the city, I never even learned my neighbours' names.

But if you're thinking of moving, be realistic. We had to buy a second car, because my partner works shifts and the last bus back from Brayminster leaves at 18:30. That cost alone has wiped out most of the money we saved on our mortgage.
Would I move back? Not a chance. But I'd tell anyone thinking about it to visit on a wet Tuesday in November, not a sunny Saturday in June.
